Whereas October is recognized as Farm to School Month, a month dedicated to celebrating the education around food, school gardens, and lunch trays filled with nutrient-dense local ingredients. And whereas Farm to School programs support the connections among students, schools, and local farmers throughout Loudoun County, empowering informed food choices while strengthening the local economy. And whereas Farm to School activities, such as inclusion of

locally grown ingredients in school meals, the cultivation of school gardens, and educational farm visits can help instill lifelong healthy habits, fueling the young minds of Loudoun County. And whereas supporting local farms and food systems promotes agricultural literacy, increases economic opportunities for local farm businesses, and builds strong regional food networks. And whereas Loudoun County Public Schools is committed to promoting wellness,

sustainability, and student engagement through education and local food initiatives. Now, therefore, be it resolved that the Loudoun County School Board officially recognizes the month of October as Farm to School Month and encourages all students and families to celebrate and participate in activities that support local food systems, healthy eating, and agricultural education. Thank you, Madam Chair. I appreciate you assigning this one to me. Whereas the Virginia General Assembly passed Senate Joint Resolution 321 in 2009, designating October as Disability History and Awareness Month in the Commonwealth of Virginia. And whereas the General Assembly recognized the importance of increasing public awareness and respect for people with disabilities, informing the

public about the many contributions to society made by people with disabilities, and emphasizing the abilities of people with disabilities. And whereas the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 was enacted to end disability-based discrimination and promote full inclusion, full participation, economic self-sufficiency, and equality of opportunity for all people with disabilities.

And whereas Loudoun families include one or more family members with a disability who meaningfully contribute to and enrich the lives of their family members as well as the Loudoun community. And whereas in the '26-27 school year, Loudoun County Public Schools is serving approximately 10,444 students with disabilities under the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act. Whereas Loudoun County Public Schools teachers and related

service providers, administrators, and staff are working collaboratively to use effective teaching approaches and related educational intervention strategies to support the unique learning needs of all students with disabilities. And whereas research has shown that students with disabilities encounter more difficulty being accepted by their peers, making friends, and being involved in school and community-based clubs

compared to students without disabilities. And whereas in Loudoun County Public Schools, more than 72.88% of students with disabilities, excuse me, spend more than 80% of their time in the general education setting where inclusive practices are promoted. And whereas the Individualized Education Plan, or IEP, an important

blueprint for all schools' educators and leaders, includes the expectation that students with disabilities pursue high academic standards, which is reflected by the greater than 95% of students with disabilities graduating on time and with more than 88.6% of the students continuing on to gainful employment, college, or other post-secondary educational opportunities

during the '25-26 school year. And whereas all Loudoun County Public School students with disabilities need, deserve, and have the potential to excel by receiving support, understanding, acceptance, and being meaningfully included in the life of their school community. And whereas Disability History and Awareness Month is an opportunity to acknowledge educators

specializing in the effective teaching strategies and to celebrate the perseverance and many achievements of adolescent students, adults with disabilities. Now therefore be it resolved that the Loudoun County Public School Board does hereby proclaim the month of October 2026 as Disability History and Awareness Month, and resolves to support increased appreciation, respect, and inclusion for people with disabilities.

And be it further resolved that Loudoun County Public Schools supports informing the school community and the public concerning the many valuable contributions to the school environment and to society made by people with disabilities. And be it further resolved that Loudoun County Public Schools principals, administrators, and educators are encouraged through education and other appropriate activities, programs, and events to promote and highlight Disability History and Awareness Month

in the Commonwealth of Virginia, as well as the value that people with disabilities bring to their specific schools and communities. And in witness thereof, that a copy of this resolution will be sent to each Loudoun County Public School so that it may be discussed, shared, and prominently displayed online and in the school during the month of October. And so that principals, administrators, and educators may

plan disability awareness activities to increase inclusion and acceptance of students with disabilities throughout all of Loudoun County Public Schools. Resolved finally, that a copy of this resolution will be sent to each Loudoun County Public School so that it may be discussed and shared and prominently displayed online in the school during the month of October so that principals, administrators, and

educators may plan disability awareness activities to increase inclusion and acceptance of students with disabilities throughout all LCPS. Thank you, Ms. LaBelle. Our next proclamation is the Domestic and Dating Violence Awareness Month Proclamation presented by Vice Chair Donahue. Thank you, Madam Chair. Whereas October is Domestic and Dating Violence Awareness Month and calls attention to the fact that dating and domestic violence are widespread and their effects impact our community.

And whereas domestic violence affects one in three women and one in four men in their lifetime. In addition, one in 12 high school students has experienced violence in a dating relationship Domestic violence and dating relationship violence cause harm to thousands of Virginians regardless of their age, race, sexual orientation, religion, gender identity, or socioeconomic status. And whereas during Domestic and Dating Violence Awareness Month, we honor survivors and provide public awareness on

this violation of the basic human right to be free from violence and abuse, removing the stigma and shame surrounding such violence, expanding support for survivors of sexual violence, and strengthening our response. And whereas although progress has been made toward preventing and ending domestic and dating violence and providing support to survivors and their families, important work remains to be done. In particular, a focus on teaching the community about healthy relationships to help reduce the likelihood of dating partner violence.

And whereas Loudoun County Public Schools and LAWS Domestic Violence and Sexual Assault Services work together to name the current challenges to addressing violence, identify strategies to address risk factors, and implement solutions to stop violence before it happens. And whereas recognizing that the trauma sustained from experiencing domestic or dating relationship violence is not something that someone gets over, it is something that someone survives. Loudoun County Public Schools is committed to raising

awareness about healthy relationships and body safety, taking ownership in prevention work, and creating a culture where violence is unacceptable. Now therefore be it resolved that the Loudoun County School Board formally recognizes October 2026 as Domestic and Dating Violence Awareness Month, a time in our community to create safety for children, youth, faculty, staff, and families in Loudoun County Public Schools. Working together, we encourage our community to share information about domestic

and dating violence prevention, support survivors, and speak out against harmful attitudes and actions, joining advocates and communities across the Commonwealth and the country in playing an active role to prevent domestic and dating violence. Thank you, Chair Chandler and board members, Dr. Spence. Mr. Smith and I are thankful for the opportunity to provide the board and the public an update on some work that is happening around intentional instructional technology in LCPS. Starting tonight, we are here together as the Departments of Digital Innovation and Teaching and Learning work together to deliver on

this vision. Our work bridges instructional strategy and technical execution. The Department of Teaching and Learning leads our curriculum design and teaching integration, while our dedicated technical teams across DDI manage the underlying systems and resolve support issues. I'd like to take a moment and recognize a number of members of the team joining us this afternoon. First, our Director of Professional Growth and Innovation, Nicole Lagoni. We also have Instructional Technology Supervisors Mike Henrickson and

Chana Pribek. And I'd also like to recognize Lori Sink, our Program Manager in Teaching and Learning, helping with much of the lift in this area. And I know there are members of DDI here as well. Thank you, Mr. Slepin. So DDI's role is really to provide that technical support to support the instructional vision of our teaching and learning team. So our team is here to really provide that sustainable framework that we can rely upon every single day to ensure that instruction is delivered using technology. And I would just like to recognize Mr.

Justin Donovan here, who is our Director of Digital Experience. Today's update centers on four core areas: what's new this year in our approach to digital learning environments, what data is available to guide decision-making related to these environments, and then an update on two steps we are taking to pilot what our classrooms might look like in the future. The overarching thread connecting all four is intentionality,

ensuring technology is used when and how it truly enhances student learning. First, to align our efforts division-wide, we published our instructional technology guidance, establishing a clear vision for how tech supports student learning. This document serves as a foundation for staff development days, anchors our leadership and ITF training and support, and is shared on our public student tech site so families have full visibility into our

beliefs and philosophy around instructional technology. It outlines the division-wide vision for how technology supports student learning. It establishes the why behind our use of technology, whether it's for access, differentiation, or learning in support of the LCPS profile of a graduate. It shares guidance on how to think about screen time and sets expectations for it in our elementary classroom. It provides public transparency for families and resources available via the

student technology website, and it guides training for school leaders and instructional technology facilitators. This document's also available to each of you in your board packet for tonight. Second foundational approach that we are considering is to provide consistency across our schools. Our Library Media Services and Instructional Technology Office partnered to update our digital citizenship and AI literacy scope and sequence this year.

Each grade level uses targeted Common Sense Media and LCPS-created lessons, while dedicated school implementation teams meet regularly with division staff to support planning and implementation of these lessons. So we have updated our digital citizenship and AI literacy scope through a joint effort between our teams. We have standardized grade-level lessons to make sure there's consistency and we know what is happening at the school level, and we've also established school-based digital literacy implementations teams to

support school leadership in meeting this goal for our school system. Accessibility continues to be a focus for the division as we help teachers and staff create accessible content through instructional technology. We launched a new required module for staff to learn about accessibility requirements under Title II of ADA. We are adopting new tools to make workflows easier, including integrating an accessibility tool into Schoology.

Staff can also use these tools as a standalone accessibility checker to remediate PDFs and other common file types while sharing with the community. Division staff are continuing to build out resources to support teachers and staff with creating accessible content. We will now transition to changes or refinements that were implemented for the start of this school year. So this slide outlines some changes that were implemented before the start of school. These include Chromebook carts.

The school board directed DDI to provide Chromebook carts to grade one classrooms. That was completed before the start of school. So as of now, all kindergarten and grade one classrooms have carts in those classrooms for those devices to stay at school and have a place where they are managed away from the student. We also removed direct access to YouTube and Gmail for our students in grades three through five. So students in grades K through two already did not have access to these resources. And after review,

Gmail was not heavily used by our students in grades three through five. So that was disabled and really based off of feedback that we received to help provide additional focus, and reduce distractions in the classroom to remove students' direct access to YouTube content. Students still have access to instructional content that the teacher can provide access to or direct them to or show them, but they do not have that direct access to just watch any video that they would choose. We adopted Note

as a division-wide study and practice tool. So previously, we had several available or freemium versions where we did not have licensing or contracts in place. That included tools like Quizlet, if the board had received any questions or comments about that. Quizlet did not meet our data privacy standards, so we have embraced Note as a division, and we have contractual and data protection agreements in place to ensure that it is used appropriately. The last item on the list here is the adoption of Aptigy Rooms and Phoenix Pass.

Really the goal of reducing application sprawl, making sure that our dollars are being used as appropriate as possible, and leveraging existing functionality inside of platforms that we already own and use throughout the division. Next, we'll get into screen time. I know this has been a very popular topic. So this report here, which is pulled from our LightSpeed content filter. So every device across the division, staff and

student, has an agent built into it that tracks what they do on the internet, and then this is that backend report that we're able to pull. This report shows It's from August 17th, which was the first day of school, through September 11th, when I pulled the report, and really just want to make sure they understand what it's showing. If a student uses a device on a day, this is how long they've used that device for. So you see here, kindergarten is 22 minutes. That doesn't mean a kindergarten student uses a device 22 minutes every day.

It means on the days when they use technology, they average 22 minutes total, and that is a daily use metric. So if it's seven minutes in the morning and 15 minutes in the afternoon, it's 22 minutes for the day. So the way the vendor has developed this report is so that screen time doesn't get diluted by student absences or school closures, or days when students aren't in school, that it really is when they use the technology, how long are they using it for, and how long are they engaged with it?

On the next slide, this is the same report pulled, but limited to only the 13 schools that are in the Smart Start K through 2 pilot. So you can see here about a 28% to 32% reduction in screen time use at those schools. So kindergarten is at 13 minutes, first grade is 21 minutes, second grade is 33 minutes. Again, that is only when they engage with technology. So we see reduced devices at those locations, but also more

intentional use of that technology when those devices are in use. This slide shows our top apps so far over the past 30 days. Really, ClassLink is LCPS Go, as everyone knows it. It is our portal to launch. So every student goes to LCPS Go, and then they go to another application, so it's always the number one, and it far exceeds everything else. But then from there, you can see Magma Math, Lexia Core, Epic Books, Clever, which is another rostering integration

that we use. And this is only for K through 2, showing those usages really of instructional applications. So breaking this further down by grade level, this table of apps helps us get a small window into the types of classroom activities where students are using technology, referring back to the instructional technology guidance. We could see examples that would indicate a range of the three different levels I had mentioned previously.

Tools like Epic or Pebble Go might indicate that students are leveraging the technology to access resources and information like e-books or content. Tools like differentiated instruction targeted at specific needs and readiness levels. And tools like Google Drive or Wixie might indicate that students are using technology for collaboration and creativity, two of our five Cs.

The availability of tools and resources is an important conversation and one of importance to our teachers and staff. As such, LCPS is implementing a new software management platform to help teachers and staff identify and select appropriate instructional tools. Helping teachers identify and select appropriate instructional tools, and then determining how best to implement those tools in the classroom is a core function of our instructional technology team and school-based instructional technology

facilitators. The new catalog is a built-in platform that allows us to have a more tailored experience for our staff when they're seeking out information. It includes better controls about what information is shared with a specific audience, better searching and filtering features, and options for sharing resources and support materials. The goal is to create a hub that can not only help teachers know what tools are available, but also to get a leg up in learning how to use these tools in the classroom.

Ultimately, we want to drive use of existing tools and help teachers recognize the extent of options already available to them, rather than them having to find and use new or unreviewed resources. Both Mr. Smith and I know this is an important thing for schools and teachers. They like what they like. But as we are trying to support and maintain this environment, we need to think at our level around protecting

student data and privacy. The more our data is out there amongst different tools, the more risk there is. We want better value and outcomes for the dollars we spend. We're very fortunate in Loudoun to be supported with a diverse set of instruction materials. We want to make sure teachers are using what has been selected through our policies and processes. We want to make sure technology access is simplified for teachers and students, they know what to use and when,

and we want to improve instructional quality and consistency through the support we provide for the tools that they have. And at the end of the day, we want to reduce cybersecurity and operational risk. Moving on to two areas where we have an opportunity to be thoughtful, but also to innovate. First, we'll start talking a little bit about where we are when it comes to student use of generative AI and AI generally in Loudoun. We know this is another topic very near and dear to our families and our

teachers. And second, we're going to give you a little bit of information on our Smart Start Tech pilot that we've talked about. Recent research from Common Sense Media shows that 86% of students aged nine to 17 have already interacted with AI in some form. The critical question for us as a division isn't whether or not students will encounter or use AI, but how are we proactively equipping them to use it safely, ethically,

and responsibly as a part of their learning? Again, 86% of youth ages nine to 17 have used AI tools. We want to shift the conversation from completely avoiding the technology to thoughtfully and actively guiding student exposure if that's the case. Why is this important? AI literacy is becoming a part of basic literacy.

Our responsibility is not simply to give access to AI, to simply turn it on, but to teach them how to use it responsibly, critically, ethically, and effectively. The goal is not to replace student thinking, but rather to strengthen it. Students should learn when AI can help them brainstorm, investigate, revise, communicate, and solve problems, and also when they need to be thinking independently and by themselves. We know students are already encountering these tools.

Avoiding Gen AI in school completely does not prepare students to navigate it. Explicit instruction gives us an opportunity to establish expectations around academic integrity, privacy, attribution, bias, accuracy, and appropriate use. AI makes critical thinking more important, not less. Because AI can produce convincing but inaccurate information, students need stronger skills in evaluating claims, checking sources, recognizing bias,

and verifying evidence. An AI-ready graduate, as this vision up here shows, is more than someone who knows how to write a prompt. As the ISTE ACSD framework illustrates, there are enduring skills that can extend well beyond any particular AI product. Human skills still need to remain at the center of anything we do when it comes to student use of generative AI. Collaboration, creativity, critical thinking, contribution, communication, those should all be familiar to us, our

profile of a graduate. Those are essential and increasingly valuable as this powerful technology becomes more and more ubiquitous and available to our students. This is also an equity issue. If schools don't deliberately teach AI literacy, students whose families or communities already understand these technologies will have an advantage. Schools can help ensure that every student learns how to use AI thoughtfully and safely. A question shouldn't simply be should students use AI? And that's a question we're having.

We're discussing about how and what that would look like. A more useful question is what do we want our graduates to be able to do in a world where AI exists, so when they leave our school system? Our curriculum and classrooms should prepare them for that world. So, in that vein, to lead in instruction while keeping pace with this technology, LCPS has established a clear and proactive positive framework when it comes to generative AI.

Early on, a number of years ago, we launched the LCPS Generative AI Guide to support safe classroom integration alongside an official gen AI policy that defines clear division-wide standards for responsible use. LCPS has had this policy in place since 2025, and many other school divisions are looking at Loudoun as a model in terms of how we're approaching this, and some are still in community conversations and developing a policy. The policy establishes clear, proactive guidelines and frameworks to keep pace with

the technological advancements, includes the philosophy, emphasizes the importance of keeping that student, the human in the center. It offers dos and don'ts for the use of technology, and we have accompanying regulation for appropriate use and data privacy. Knowing that, and to operationalize responsible use, we have launched an opt-in pilot for secondary schools using Gemini Notebook, a

tool specifically grounded in LCPS data protections. Eight participating middle and high schools will engage in targeted professional learning covering digital literacy, communication planning, and classroom integration strategies. We do not have this turned on right now, but when we go through a series of meetings and the schools are feeling ready, we plan on turning it on at some point this year. LCPS already has access to generative AI tools in more limited ways.

In instances where vendors have added generative AI features, we evaluate to ensure student safety and adequate oversight, and we have enabled access for students only where generative AI tools are heavily guardrailed or narrow in scope when teachers have direct insight and oversight to how students are using these tools.

Moving on to our Smart Start K-2 tech pilot. In LCPS, instructional technology must serve as purposeful support for learning, which is why we are partnering with elementary schools to evaluate our current K-2 device models. Based on recent data regarding screen time and application usage, the Department of Teaching and Learning and Digital Innovation are partnering with elementary schools to rethink the traditional one-to-one device deployment in grades K-2.

Instead of assigning individual devices to every student, participating schools are exploring alternative models. The goal is to promote purposeful engagement, designing active learning experiences that emphasize tactile learning and peer-to-peer interaction, while making very intentional choices about when technology meaningfully enhances the instruction happening in the classroom. This pilot is being fully co-created between our central office teams and school leadership. The primary requirement for

participation was and is strong teacher buy-in. We want to work alongside our schools and our school leaders and our K-2 teams to gather honest, reflective feedback on how reduced devices impact instruction, assessment, intervention, learning outcomes, and teacher workload. So on the screen are our 13 partners. I do just want to extend a heartfelt thank you to the principals who took a risk in having this conversation with their staff, the

teachers, the CLTs, and the ITFs are leaning in on this work, in terms of helping us work through some of the speed bumps that have come along with trying something old but new, in terms of how we're approaching instruction in our classrooms. As Mr. Slevin said, we really wanted to partner with these 13 schools and not have something prescriptive that everyone was going to do the same. So each of these schools have reviewed what they think would work best for them.

And we have different deployment models that we're evaluating. So some of them are using a shared cart, say, three first-grade classrooms are sharing a single cart. Some of them are doing smaller classroom sets, say, six devices in a classroom versus the cart being shared. There's a combination of both of those. We have different size schools, so we try to choose schools that had many different classrooms. Those were smaller schools with maybe a single first grade and kindergarten classroom, and really get an idea of what that would look like at the school level, and we're continuing to collect that feedback.

So we are beginning to gather some feedback, and all of our schools are still in the pilot, so appreciate that. And some positives. And there is positive feedback from our teachers and our principals in terms of having them rethink creative solutions and new ways of organizing resources around technology and their time. Mean time is the number one resource in an elementary classroom. There is strong collaboration amongst the teams.

We have regular check-ins with the ITS and the principals and optional calls, where teachers and principals can voice what their needs are. And there is a real commitment to supporting the intentional use of technology. And our principals are really demonstrating they understand the moment we're in and the conversation that we need to be having as a school system. There have been challenges as we are relearning some of, like I said, old habits in terms of shared devices, scheduling carts.

There is a certain level of efficiency that comes with the deployment model that we currently have. And that has centered mostly around delivering intervention and personalized practice. And that, in many ways, is not only on the teacher teams or the CLTs, but also the guidance we're giving centrally, how we're working with them in terms of our expectations for use.
